description: We created Canary, a platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to monitor astronauts’ physical and mental health during space missions. It tracks vital signs, sleep, stress, mood, and cognitive performance, comparing each astronaut’s data with their personal baseline to detect potential health risks. The system also provides personalized recommendations, emergency guidance, and a 3D human body visualization, supporting crew safety and well-being during long-duration missions.
summary:
Miners used to take canaries underground. The bird felt bad air before they did. Astronauts need one too.Long missions expose astronauts to NASA’s five spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity and closed environments, bringing immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events and behavioral problems. Near Mars, messages to Earth take up to 24 minutes each way, so astronauts must spot these changes themselves.

Canary is an offline, on-board software prototype. Astronauts log heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, mood and cognitive tests; sensors and labs add blood sugar, blood counts and radiation dose. Canary compares each person with their own normal, catches signals that move together, turns warnings into small goals and checks whether they worked. A clickable 3D body colors each system by status and explains what it means, what to do and how to measure it, with trend charts and goals that reward participation.

Explainable rules decide, each limit sourced (NASA-STD-3001 included); AI only explains. Amber brings simple goals; red alerts the medical officer and Earth; emergencies get step-by-step guidance. Rules adapt to the station, Moon, rover or Mars. NASA data: Inspiration4 bloodwork, DONKI solar storms and Curiosity radiation; the rest is simulated and labeled.

With Canary, astronauts act without waiting for Earth, and remote communities could benefit too.
details:
What it does and how it works

Miners used to take canaries underground because the bird felt bad air before they did. We wanted that for a crew on its way to Mars.

Canary runs on the ship, with no internet, and works in three steps: Learn, Monitor, Respond.

Learn. Every astronaut is different, so the system doesn’t compare anyone with an average. Before launch it learns each person’s own normal. Data comes in a few ways. There are tests in the app itself: reaction time, processing speed, memory, mood, sleep, sleepiness, workload. There are vital signs, which the astronaut types in and can back up with a photo of the device’s display. And there are sensor readings and blood tests, which come in through their own route. Every piece of data knows where it came from: NASA, the simulation, or the astronaut.

Monitor. Every value is checked against the person’s normal, against the normal range for the population, and against the limits in NASA’s spaceflight health standard, NASA-STD-3001. That gives a color: green, amber or red. Related signals add up to eight risks. Four of them are the ones NASA rates as most serious for Mars: radiation, vision, behavioral health and nutrition (Patel et al., 2020). The rules change with the place. On the ship, on the Moon or on Mars, gravity and radiation are different, and the system knows that.

The case we use in the demo is Helena, a made-up crew member. On day 147 she’s sleeping less, reacting more slowly, feeling down and spending less time with the rest of the crew. Look at each number on its own and nothing stands out. Canary notices they’re all dropping together, and her brain turns red on the 3D body.

Respond. A warning only helps if you know what to do about it. At amber, Canary suggests small goals, like protecting your sleep window, and sets a day to check whether things got better. If two tries in a row don’t work, it calls the medical officer on board. At red, the medical officer is told right away and a summary goes to Earth. For emergencies there’s a button that opens step-by-step guidance, different in zero gravity, on the Moon, on Mars or on Earth. And Ask Canary explains all of this in plain words.

Benefits

On the ISS the crew can talk to the flight surgeon almost in real time. On the way to Mars, a single question can take 48 minutes to get an answer. Canary is for that gap. Astronauts understand what’s going on with their own body, because each part of the 3D body explains what it means, what to do and how to measure it. The medical officer gets a triage that’s already sorted. And because the rules are fixed and every limit has a source, the medical team can review them and change whatever they want.

Intended impact

We thought about Mars first, but the same logic works for the ISS and the Moon. It also works for people far from a hospital here on Earth: ship crews, oil platforms, Antarctic bases. There’s still a lot to do before this is real. The protocols need review by flight surgeons, it needs to connect to real devices, and it needs to sync with a ground station. The data side is ready for that already: when real data shows up, it replaces the simulated data without touching the code.

Tools

Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js

3D body: MakeHuman (CC0) and BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA), converted with our own scripts

Data: Python scripts for the NASA data and a generator for the simulated data

AI (Ask Canary): Gemini Flash 3.1

Tests: About 400 automated tests

Hardware: None. A wristband, a blood pressure cuff and an on-board blood analyzer stayed as the idea of how data would be collected on a real mission

Creativity

The canary idea drove the whole project, from the name to the opening of the video. The part that feels most like ours is that the system comes back to check whether the advice worked, instead of firing an alert and stopping there. Another thing we like: NASA’s limits depend on the place. Tomás, another character in the demo, is fit enough for a spacewalk from the ship, but not for walking on the surface of Mars. So the same number shows up yellow in one place and red in the other.

What the team considered

The rule that mattered most: the system talks about risk and doesn’t diagnose. Fixed rules decide the alerts; the AI only explains.

We also thought about false alarms. One bad night doesn’t turn anyone red. That takes three signals, and they have to last more than a day. And we thought about the crew’s time, so the tests take a few minutes and show up as daily goals.

Privacy took a lot of discussion. Each person’s data stays with them and the medical team. Halfway through we realized the goals ranking was telling everyone Helena wasn’t doing well, because she dropped to last place. We changed it to count only routine goals, and the goals that come from an alert stay private.

The NASA data had some surprises. In the Inspiration4 blood count file (OSD-569), one crew member’s values at one collection were shifted by a row. We checked it with the math (white cells times percentage) and lined them back up. Before that, the system thought she already had abnormal lymphocytes before the flight and ignored a real drop. We left out the glucose from the metabolic panel (OSD-575) on purpose: three of the four crew members show very low values on the same day, which looks like samples that were processed late. And we noticed everyone was being compared with the male range, so we switched to the lab’s range for each sex.

Other than that, the data is simulated, because astronaut health data from flight isn’t public. Everything simulated is labeled that way, and numbers without a source are marked as our own assumptions. The emergency protocols are illustrative and would need a flight surgeon to sign off on them.
